rationale: B wins because it finds the sharper conflict, not just the cleaner announcement frame. "What 40 chain optometry clinics mean for the independent eye doctor down the street" gives a reporter a real antagonist and a reason to call critics; A's "Warby Parker bets its next 40 stores on the optometrist, not the eyewear wall" is strong, but more company-centered. Both sets know where the bodies are buried, but B is more useful to a founder because it shows the least flattering viable story before a reporter does.
gaps_in_A: "LensCrafters, EssilorLuxottica, Pearle Vision" imports named competitors not supplied in the update; useful context, but the set should mark that as outside reporting, not treated fact.
"the historically defensible, insurance-tied part of the optical business" is plausible, but not grounded in the provided facts and needs sourcing before it anchors the lead angle.
"A DTC eyewear brand" and "started as a glasses-by-mail disruptor" rely on background not in the update. Less fatal than B's DTC thesis, but still unclean under the rules.
The pharmacy angle admits its own weakness: "an unnamed-partner pilot has almost no reportable detail yet." Keeping it is fine, but it is filler until the partner and scope exist.
gaps_in_B: "proved you don't need stores" and "canonical case study" are not in the update. That is pundit shorthand dressed as evidence.
"40 chain optometry clinics" overstates the facts. The update says most new stores will offer optometrist-staffed exams; it does not say all 40 are clinics.

"A profitable Warby Parker won't say what its eye exams earn" turns "exam-revenue contribution not broken out" into a slightly prosecutorial claim. Good angle, but the wording needs legal-clean restraint.

"shift of routine vision care out of independent optometry practices and into national retail chains" is a real story only with outside proof. B asks for some of it, but the headline-level premise outruns the supplied facts.
